title: How a Hole Becomes a Subway

beats.say: You're tired of sitting in traffic, so you grab a shovel and dig a hole straight down.
Congratulations, you've built a subway. It goes nowhere, and a raccoon already lives in it.
Your friend Gary climbs in to inspect it, and the walls instantly cave in. Gary is now a fossil.
So you dig him out and brace the walls with planks and beams. This is called shoring. It stops the ground from giving Gary a hug he can't escape.
You dig deeper, and suddenly water pours in. You've hit the water table, where the ground is basically a soggy sponge. Gary is now doing the backstroke.
So you install pumps that never stop. New York's subway pumps out about 13 million gallons of water on a dry day.
Now you just have to dig sideways across town. With one shovel, that takes about 100 years. Gary's beard is already touching the floor.
So you bring in a tunnel boring machine: a giant spinning cheese grater longer than a football field. It chews through about 50 feet of dirt a day.
Unfortunately, that dirt was holding up the bakery above you. This is called settlement. The bakery is now sinking into your tunnel, croissants first.
So right behind the cutter, the machine bolts concrete rings into place. Each one weighs 60 tons and holds the street up like a giant concrete donut.
But the tunnel is miles long, the air is awful, and Gary just passed out next to a pigeon. So you add ventilation shafts with giant fans that pull fresh air down from the street.
Next, the trains need power, so you add a third rail carrying 625 volts. Don't touch it, Gary. Gary touched it.
Add stations, escalators, turnstiles, a map nobody understands, and one mysterious puddle that never dries.

Congratulations, you've built a subway. You started with a shovel because you hated traffic. Now it costs over 4 billion dollars a mile, every ride is 3 dollars, and Gary is stuck in the turnstile. The raccoon rides free.
